title: Pandas Essentials: Series, DataFrame, loc/iloc and Filtering
summary: Quick revision notes on pandas' two core structures, loading and inspecting CSV data, selecting with loc and iloc, boolean filtering and index control. Ends with the common mistakes and a cheat sheet.

chapters.title: Series and DataFrame Mental Model
points: Series = 1-D labelled array: values plus an index, with one dtype for the whole Series
DataFrame = 2-D table; each column is a Series and all columns share one row index
Build from a dict of columns: pd.DataFrame({'name': ['A','B'], 'age': [30, 25]}); keys become column names
Index labels are used for alignment: s1 + s2 matches by label, and missing labels give NaN
df.shape gives (rows, cols), df.dtypes gives the type per column, df.columns and df.index give the labels

chapters.title: Loading and Inspecting Data
points: df = pd.read_csv('file.csv') reads a CSV; useful args are sep=';', usecols=[...], dtype={...}, parse_dates=['date'], nrows=1000
df.head(n) and df.tail(n) show the first or last n rows (default 5); use them as a first sanity check
df.info() prints the column dtypes, non-null counts and memory use; a non-null count below the row count means missing values
df.describe() summarises numeric columns only (count, mean, std, min, quartiles, max); describe(include='all') adds the non-numeric columns (text columns are str dtype in pandas 3)
Check missing values with df.isna().sum(), and check unique values with df['col'].nunique() and df['col'].value_counts()

chapters.title: Selecting Columns, loc vs iloc
points: df['col'] returns a Series; df[['a','b']] (a list) returns a DataFrame
df.loc[rows, cols] selects by label; slices are inclusive of the end: df.loc[0:2] returns 3 rows
df.iloc[rows, cols] selects by integer position; slices exclude the end: df.iloc[0:2] returns 2 rows
Examples: df.loc[5, 'age'] (label), df.iloc[0, 1] (position), df.loc[:, 'a':'c'] (all rows, columns a to c)
Prefer loc/iloc for assignment, e.g. df.loc[df['age'] > 30, 'senior'] = True; avoid chained indexing like df[...]['col'] = x

chapters.title: Boolean Filtering and Index Control
points: df[df['age'] > 30] builds a boolean Series mask and keeps only the rows where it is True
Combine conditions with & (and), | (or) and ~ (not), wrapping each condition in parentheses: df[(df.age > 30) & (df.city == 'NYC')]
Membership and text filters: df[df['city'].isin(['NYC','LA'])], df[df['name'].str.contains('an')]
df.set_index('id') makes a column the index (returns a new DataFrame); df.loc[101] then looks up by that label
df.reset_index(drop=True) restores 0..n-1 after filtering or sorting; without drop=True the old index becomes a column

chapters.title: Common Mistakes
points: Using and/or instead of &/| in a filter raises 'truth value of a Series is ambiguous'
Forgetting the parentheses around each condition: df.age > 30 & df.x == 1 evaluates in the wrong order and fails
Chained assignment df[df.a > 1]['b'] = 0 never updates df under pandas 3 Copy-on-Write (it writes to a temporary copy and emits a ChainedAssignmentError warning); use df.loc[mask, 'b'] = 0
After filtering, the index keeps the original labels, so iloc and loc return different rows; call reset_index(drop=True) if you need positions
set_index, reset_index and drop return new objects; assign the result (df = df.set_index('id')) or the change is lost

chapters.title: Pandas Basics Cheat Sheet
points: Load and peek: pd.read_csv(path), df.head(), df.info(), df.describe(), df.shape
Columns: df['a'] gives a Series, df[['a','b']] gives a DataFrame
Rows: df.loc[label_or_mask, cols] (label, end-inclusive), df.iloc[pos, pos] (position, end-exclusive)
Filter: df[(cond1) & (cond2)], df[col.isin([...])], ~ for not
Index: df.set_index('col'), df.reset_index(drop=True); both return a new DataFrame
